chapters.title: Chapter 2: Listed Shares and Equity Mutual Funds

lessons.title: Grandfathering: Shares and Funds Bought Before 1 February 2018

body.text: Every rupee your shares and equity funds gained up to 31 January 2018 is permanently shielded from tax. Grandfathering taxes only the growth that came after that date.

children.text: Rakesh, a 58-year-old bank manager in Lucknow, bought 200 shares of a large private bank in 2014 at ₹650 each. He sold them in 2026 at ₹2,450. His broker's tax P&L showed a long-term gain of ₹1,10,000, not the ₹3,60,000 he expected from simple subtraction. The difference is grandfathering, and if you or your parents hold anything bought before February 2018, it is worth real money.

From October 2004 to March 2018, long-term gains on listed shares and equity funds were fully exempt. Budget 2018, presented on 1 February 2018, brought them back into the tax net from 1 April 2018. Taxing gains that had already built up while the law promised exemption would have been unfair, so the government froze values at the closing point just before the announcement: 31 January 2018.

body.text: The cap at sale price is the clever part. Grandfathering can shrink a gain to zero (Case B), but it can never manufacture a loss out of a stock that fell after January 2018 while still being above what you actually paid. A real loss below your actual purchase price (Case C) is still recognised.

body.title: Pick the Right Cost
body.question: Meenal bought an equity fund in 2016 at a NAV of ₹40. The NAV on 31 January 2018 was ₹58. She redeems in 2026 at a NAV of ₹52. What cost per unit is used?
body.explanation: FMV of ₹58 is capped at the sale value of ₹52, so min(58, 52) = ₹52. Then max(40, 52) = ₹52. Her cost equals her redemption value, so her gain is nil, even though she is ₹12 above her actual purchase NAV. No loss arises either.

body.title: Rakesh's Grandfathered Gain
body.prompt: Rakesh bought 200 shares in 2014 at ₹650. The highest price quoted on 31 January 2018 was ₹1,900. He sells all 200 shares in 2026 at ₹2,450. Ignoring expenses, what is his long-term capital gain in rupees?
body.explanation: Cost per share = max(₹650, min(₹1,900, ₹2,450)) = ₹1,900. Gain per share = ₹2,450 − ₹1,900 = ₹550. Total gain = ₹550 × 200 = ₹1,10,000. Prices are illustrative.

body.label: What Grandfathering Saved Rakesh
body.context: Without grandfathering, his gain would be ₹3,60,000 and tax at 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh exemption would be ₹29,375 before cess. With grandfathering, his ₹1,10,000 gain sits within the exemption, so tax is ₹0, assuming no other long-term equity gains that year.

children.text: What Is Covered and What Is Not

body.title: Grandfathering Applies Only to Section 198 Assets

columns.label: Covered
points: Listed equity shares acquired on or before 31 January 2018
Equity-oriented mutual fund units acquired on or before 31 January 2018
Listed equity ETF units acquired on or before 31 January 2018
Business trust units (REITs and InvITs) within section 198
Bonus shares allotted on or before 31 January 2018

columns.label: Not Covered
points: Anything acquired on or after 1 February 2018
Debt funds, gold, gold ETFs and international funds
Property and unlisted shares that never listed
Shares sold off-market without STT, which fall under section 197

body.title: Which Price on 31 January?
body.textWithBlank: For listed shares, the FMV used for grandfathering is the ___ price quoted on a recognised stock exchange on 31 January 2018.
body.explanation: The law uses the highest quoted price that day, not the closing price. That is slightly more generous to investors, since it gives a higher cost. Brokers usually apply this automatically in their tax P&L.

body.title: Special Cases: Bonus Shares, Later IPOs and Old SIPs

children.text: Bonus shares: bonus shares normally have nil cost. But if they were allotted on or before 31 January 2018, grandfathering applies. For 100 bonus shares with an FMV of ₹500 sold at ₹800, cost is max(₹0, min(₹500, ₹800)) = ₹500, so the gain is ₹30,000, not ₹80,000.

Shares that listed after 31 January 2018: if you bought shares of an unlisted company in 2015-16 at ₹100 and it listed through an IPO later, the deemed FMV is ₹100 × 272 ÷ 254 = ₹107.09. CII stands for cost inflation index; here it is used only to estimate a January 2018 value, not for indexation.

Old SIPs: FIFO still applies. SIP instalments bought on or before 31 January 2018 get grandfathered cost using the NAV on that date. Instalments after that use actual NAV. A single redemption can mix both.

body.title: Lakshmi's Old SIP
body.scenario: Lakshmi ran a monthly SIP in a large cap equity fund from January 2016 to December 2020. In 2026 she redeems her entire holding. The fund's NAV rose through most of that period, but NAV on 31 January 2018 was higher than several of her 2016 and 2017 purchase NAVs.
body.prompt: How will the fund house compute cost for her redemption, and which instalments benefit from grandfathering?
body.modelAnswer: The fund house redeems units lot by lot using FIFO. For every instalment from January 2016 to January 2018, cost per unit is the higher of the actual purchase NAV and the 31 January 2018 NAV, capped at the 2026 redemption NAV. Since the redemption NAV is well above the January 2018 NAV, those lots effectively get the January 2018 NAV as cost, and their pre-2018 growth is not taxed. Instalments from February 2018 to December 2020 use their actual purchase NAV. All lots are long-term, so the combined gain is taxed at 12.5% above the ₹1.25 lakh exemption.

body.label: Look Up Historical Mutual Fund NAVs on AMFI
body.description: Use AMFI's NAV history tool to check any scheme's NAV on 31 January 2018 if your capital gains statement does not show the grandfathered cost.

body.text: Your ITR asks for grandfathered long-term equity gains to be reported scrip by scrip, with the ISIN, actual cost and FMV on 31 January 2018. Keep your broker's tax P&L and fund house capital gains statements, which usually show this FMV already.

cards.definition: 31 January 2018. Values on this day protect gains built up before the LTCG tax returned.
Highest price quoted on a recognised stock exchange on 31 January 2018.
NAV on 31 January 2018 for units that are not listed.
Higher of actual cost and the lower of FMV and sale value.
Stops grandfathering from creating an artificial loss.

body.title: Check Your Pre-2018 Holdings
steps: List every share, equity fund and ETF holding bought on or before 31 January 2018, including your parents' holdings you may inherit
Confirm your broker's tax P&L or CAS shows the FMV on 31 January 2018 for those lots
For physical share certificates later dematerialised, dig out the original purchase date and cost
Before selling, compare the current price with both actual cost and January 2018 FMV to estimate the gain
Remember that gifted or inherited pre-2018 holdings still qualify, using the previous owner's date and cost

points: Grandfathering protects gains on listed equity and equity funds built up to 31 January 2018
Cost = higher of actual cost and the lower of FMV on 31 January 2018 and sale value
FMV is the highest quoted price on 31 January 2018 for listed assets and NAV for unlisted fund units
It can reduce a gain to zero but cannot create an artificial loss
It covers only section 198 assets, not debt funds, gold, property or unlisted shares that never listed
Old SIPs mix grandfathered and non-grandfathered lots, applied through FIFO
